blocks.content: Have you ever subscribed to a YouTube channel?
When the creator uploads every subscriber gets notified automatically. The creator does not call each person individually. They just upload and YouTube handles the rest.
This is the Observer Pattern.
One object changes. Everyone watching gets notified. Automatically.
Without it your code looks like this:
Every new listener means editing the same class. It never stops growing.
With Observer:

orderSubject.notifyObservers(order);
// anyone who subscribed gets notified automatically

It is useful when:

["Multiple parts of your system react to one change.","You want to add or remove listeners without touching existing code.","You need loose coupling between the object that changes and the objects that react."]
items: Multiple parts of your system react to one change.
You want to add or remove listeners without touching existing code.
You need loose coupling between the object that changes and the objects that react.

blocks.content: Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Stock Price Updates
Imagine you are building a Stock Market App. The app connects to a live stock exchange and continuously receives price updates for stocks like Apple, Google, and Tesla.
Multiple modules in your app need to react to every price change:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245807334-e15ed98a.jpg
The Naive Approach
In a straightforward implementation, StockPrice directly holds references to all dependent modules, creates them, and calls their methods every time a price changes.
Here is how the client uses it:
This works at first. But watch what happens as the app grows.
Problems With This Approach

1. Tight Coupling StockPrice directly knows about PriceDisplay, AlertService, and TradingBot. It knows their class names, their method signatures, and creates them itself. Change any one of them and StockPrice breaks.
2. Violates Open/Closed Principle Want to add a PortfolioTracker that updates the user's portfolio on every price change? Or a NewsCorrelator that links price movements to news events?
Every new feature forces you to modify StockPrice adding a new field, updating priceUpdated(), and touching a class that was already working fine.

3. Inflexible and Static Modules cannot be added or removed at runtime. What if the user turns off the trading bot in settings? You end up adding if checks inside StockPrice making it fragile and messy.

4. Responsibility Bloat StockPrice should do one thing track the current price of a stock. Instead it is also managing UI updates, alert checks, and trading decisions. It has grown into something it was never meant to be.
5. Hard to Scale Every developer adding a new feature must open priceUpdated(), understand the entire sequence, and bolt on more code. The method keeps growing with no end in sight.
What We Really Need

["StockPrice should broadcast changes without knowing who is listening.","Each module should be able to subscribe or unsubscribe at any time.","Adding a new module should never require touching StockPrice.","Each module should decide for itself how to respond to a price change."]
items: StockPrice should broadcast changes without knowing who is listening.
Each module should be able to subscribe or unsubscribe at any time.
Adding a new module should never require touching StockPrice.
Each module should decide for itself how to respond to a price change.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Observer Pattern provides.
2. Understanding the Observer Pattern

The Observer Pattern provides a clean solution to the problem of broadcasting changes from one central object the Subject to many dependent objects the Observers while keeping them completely loosely coupled.
Two characteristics define it:

1. One-to-many notification A single subject can have any number of observers. When the subject's state changes, it loops through its observer list and calls update() on each one. The subject does not know or care what each observer does with the information. It just sends the signal.
2. Loose coupling The subject only depends on the observer interface never on concrete observer classes. Observers can be added, removed, or swapped at runtime without the subject ever changing.

Real-World Analogy

Think about a cricket score app.

Millions of fans subscribe to live score updates. Every time a wicket falls or a boundary is hit, the app broadcasts the update to every subscriber instantly. 

The score system does not know whether you are watching on a phone, a laptop, or a smartwatch. It does not care. It just broadcasts and every subscriber reacts in their own way.

Cancel your subscription and updates stop. A new fan subscribes and updates start. The scoring system never changes.

The Observer Pattern works exactly the same way.

blocks.content: The Four Participants

1. Subject Interface Declares the three management methods every subject must support register(), remove(), and notifyObservers(). The subject holds a list of observers typed to the interface never to concrete classes. Any class implementing Observer can subscribe and the subject never needs to know what it is.
2. Observer Interface Declares the single update() method that the subject calls whenever its state changes. Every module that wants to react to stock price changes implements this interface.

3. ConcreteSubject StockPrice Holds the actual stock price and the list of registered observers. Whenever priceUpdated()is called, it updates its state and immediately calls notifyObservers() to broadcast the change to everyone listening.

4. ConcreteObservers PriceDisplay, AlertService, TradingBot Each implements update() and defines its own reaction to a price change. PriceDisplay refreshes the screen. AlertService checks if any user targets were hit. TradingBot evaluates whether to buy or sell. The subject knows nothing about any of this.
3. How It Works
The Observer workflow follows these steps:
Flow Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245807736-9c2da9b3.png
Step 1: The client creates a StockPrice subject and one or more observers.
Step 2: Each observer registers itself with the subject by calling register(). The subject adds it to its internal list.
Step 3: When the price changes, the subject calls notifyObservers() which loops through the list and calls update() on each observer.
Step 4: Each observer pulls the data it needs from the subject via getter methods and runs its own logic.
Step 5: To stop receiving updates an observer calls remove(). The subject drops it from the list and future notifications skip it completely.
4. Implementing Observer Pattern
Let's refactor the stock price system using the Observer Pattern step by step.
Step 1: Define the Observer Interface
Each observer receives a reference to the subject and pulls whatever data it needs. This keeps the interface stable even as StockPrice gains new fields.
Step 2: Define the Subject Interface
Step 3: Implement the ConcreteSubject
StockPrice implements the subject interface. It manages the observer list and calls notifyObservers() automatically whenever the price changes.
Notice that StockPrice no longer creates or references any concrete observer. It just maintains a list of StockObserverreferences and iterates through them.

blocks.content: What We Achieved

["Loose coupling StockPrice does not know who is listening. It just broadcasts to a list of interfaces.","Open/Closed compliance adding a PortfolioTracker only requires implementing StockObserver and calling register(). Zero changes to StockPrice.","Runtime flexibility observers can be added or removed dynamically based on user settings or feature flags.","Clean separation each observer handles its own logic. StockPrice manages prices and nothing else.","Independent testability each observer can be tested by creating a mock StockPrice and calling update() directly."]
items: Loose coupling StockPrice does not know who is listening. It just broadcasts to a list of interfaces.
Open/Closed compliance adding a PortfolioTracker only requires implementing StockObserver and calling register(). Zero changes to StockPrice.
Runtime flexibility observers can be added or removed dynamically based on user settings or feature flags.
Clean separation each observer handles its own logic. StockPrice manages prices and nothing else.
Independent testability each observer can be tested by creating a mock StockPrice and calling update() directly.

blocks.content: The real test of any pattern is what happens when requirements change. The product team wants a new feature a DailyReportGenerator that tracks how many times a stock was updated throughout the day and prints a summary.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245807951-108169e4.png
With the Observer Pattern we do not touch StockPrice at all. We just create a new observer and register it.
To use it just register it:
The key point we added a completely new feature without modifying a single line in StockPrice, PriceDisplay, AlertService, or TradingBot. This is the Open/Closed Principle in action.
6. Practical Example: Weather Station

A WeatherStation publishes live weather updates. Multiple observers react to every update a TemperatureDisplay shows the current temperature, a HumidityMonitor tracks humidity levels, and a StormAlert warns users when conditions get dangerous.
